<reason>Both sides were sharp, well-structured, and format-compliant, and A had the flashier rhetoric and a genuinely original frame ("penalty wearing a spreadsheet," the tribe-vs-cost attack). But the debate resolved on two clashes B won. First, the textual clash A made central: the motion's own conditional clause ("when their size imposes higher... costs") is the cost trigger, and "oversized" is itself a size descriptor, so B's defense — anchored in that text, including the direct "Yes" on the EV-sedan question plus a weight-and-geometry schedule that lands on SUVs and pickups — read the motion as written, while A's "you defended a different policy" charge required treating the cost clause as decoration. B then weaponized A's own A4.5 concession (cost-keyed pricing acceptable in principle), shrinking A's case to a labeling complaint. Second, alternatives: B's point that design standards are federal levers cities don't hold, arriving late and covering less harm, was never answered, while A's best hits (registration fees' blindness to exposure, no safety earmark, trivial pavement wear at passenger weights) were partially or adequately answered — exposure by the per-use nature of parking/curb fees, earmark by the price-signal response. A's pavement point stood but was low-stakes. B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1's direct "Yes" to A's EV-sedan pressure question, immediately grounded in the motion's cost trigger and the weight-plus-geometry schedule, neutralized the culture-war frame at its strongest moment; compounded by B5.1 converting A's A4.5 concession into the admission that the dispute was a label, not a principle. B2.4's "levers cities don't hold" against the design-standards alternative also went permanently unanswered.</best_rebuttal>
